title: The Philippine Immigration Detention Center: If You Don't Pay, Your Deportation Never Moves
dek: A Chinese surfer was locked up in the Philippines for 41 days. What he saw wasn't a prison — it was a business with prices posted on everything: beds, boxed meals, phones, lawyer fees. Every single thing had to be bought. Those who didn't pay were held for years, even over a decade.
why: Part of StoryFM's Behind Bars series. Medium information density but solid detail. The first half is a personal ordeal; the second half — the gang economy inside the detention center, the ransom quotes from scam companies, the lawyers jacking up prices on the spot — is where the real value is.
who: Founders and going-global operators interested in the situation of overseas Chinese, the Philippine business environment, and the corruption machinery linking gray industries to the immigration bureau.
skip: 6:29-9:14 — the surfing career and startup background, unrelated to the core mechanism.

points.h: The immigration bureau quoted 1.5 million pesos for immediate release
points.body: The night Feili was arrested, immigration officials pulled him aside and whispered, "I can help you." After talking to a lawyer, the feedback came back: hand over 1.5 million pesos, roughly 160,000-170,000 RMB, and you walk out immediately, no problem at all. Of the 12 to 13 people arrested in the same batch, nobody agreed to pay. Everyone thought it was impossible that such a thing could still exist in 2026, and wanted to resolve it through normal legal channels. But the price of refusing was this: they were transferred from the holding cells of the General City police station to the Manila Immigration Bureau's main detention center, where Feili ultimately spent 41 days.

points.h: When his phone was confiscated, the money in Gcash was transferred out
points.body: When Feili was detained his phone was taken, and they asked for his unlock code. He assumed it was standard procedure and gave it. His phone unlock code was the same as his Gcash payment password — the Philippine equivalent of Alipay. For the next four or five days he applied repeatedly and couldn't get the phone back, until he kept pressuring the Chinese consulate and his lawyer, and it was finally returned. When he turned it on, the interface had all switched to English, and the Gcash transfer records showed money had been sent out — but then transferred back the night before he got the phone. There was only about 1,000 RMB in there. Feili said it wasn't about the amount; it was that the phone had been tampered with while it wasn't in his hands. He reasoned that many Chinese in Manila working in gray-industry scams who get arrested go through this same layer of fleecing, but they don't dare go to the Chinese consulate, because their phones contain a mass of criminal evidence.

points.h: The air conditioning and takeout the immigration bureau promised were just another form
points.body: For those unwilling to buy their own plane ticket for the transfer, the immigration bureau would work on them in shifts, saying the Manila immigration facilities were excellent — air conditioning, lots of freedom, you can work out, play basketball, order takeout, use your phone. Feili said they weren't lying: there really was air conditioning, you really could order takeout — it was just another form, a completely different form. They arrived at the main detention center at past three in the morning. Getting out of the vehicle, what he saw was a square area, an outer layer of iron grating, a sheet-metal roof above, and all around it iron cages like dog kennels, with long communal sleeping platforms inside, hundreds of people. At past three in the morning many weren't sleeping — bare-chested, in nothing but underwear, they clung to the iron cages staring at the newcomers. Feili said the few foreigners said nothing for several minutes after getting out, then it hit them: they'd been lied to by the immigration bureau.

points.h: The detention center is a business invested in by a Chinese boss
points.body: What Feili heard inside was that this immigration detention center was invested in by a Chinese boss, in cooperation with the immigration bureau, and that the beds, toilets and other facilities had all been newly built by the Chinese boss. Foreigners could just stay, but Chinese who came in had to pay. The lowest-tier communal platform bed was 10,000 pesos a month, about 1,100-1,200 RMB. Wealthy "pan zong" bosses and gambling kingpins could pay 50,000 pesos a month, over 6,000 RMB, for a so-called "air-conditioned room" — in reality the bed was the same, just wrapped in tin foil and wooden boards, with a foam box of ice beside it, a hole cut in the box, and an exhaust fan drawing the cold air into the bed. That's where the immigration bureau's earlier claim that "there's air conditioning inside" came from.

points.h: Chinese gangs collect protection money: you want out without paying?
points.body: On Feili's first day inside, the head of the Chinese gang came to collect a "rumor fee," saying the facilities were all their investment and there was no way you could stay for free. Feili said he had no money, he was here to serve time, how could he be expected to pay on top of that. The gang boss, in a threatening tone, said: you're already in here and don't want to spend money, and you still think you're getting out? Feili learned that the place is run by gangs, and the Chinese gang monopolizes all the food, clothing and daily life of the Chinese, running a Chinese restaurant and a Chinese supermarket. The whole detention center held about 200 people; when Feili arrived it was the off-season, and there were still over 100 Chinese, more than half of them in gambling and gray industries. The Chinese gang's staff were paid wages — the head chef 10,000 pesos a month, kitchen hands 5,000 pesos — very low wages, but many people couldn't get out precisely because they had no money for a lawyer, so they could only work to earn.

points.h: A young man from Yunnan held over a year; his family thought he'd died in Southeast Asia
points.body: A young man from Yunnan asked Feili for help. Before the pandemic he'd been lured to the Philippines by a high-salary recruitment ad; the moment he landed his phone and passport were taken, and he was dragged into a compound to do telecom fraud. With poor performance he was shocked with an electric baton by his supervisor every day. After the company was busted he served a few months, then was transferred to the immigration detention center. The normal deportation procedure is simple — a few departments sign off, you buy your own plane ticket, and you're gone — but the immigration bureau, in order to extract money, keeps you locked up a long time; without paying, the procedure doesn't move. He'd already been held over a year, with not a cent, no phone, eating only prison food every day, unable to reach his family, who thought he'd died in Southeast Asia. Feili helped him write a letter in Chinese, translated it into English, and through an introduction from a Japanese man got to see the warden. The warden had a guard bring Feili's phone, and let the young man add his father on WeChat and send a selfie and a voice message. Afterwards the immigration bureau bought a basic phone specifically to solve this problem.

points.h: Scam company ransom: 3 million pesos per person
points.body: The only Chinese person Feili talked with at any length was from a scam company. The company's seventy or eighty people had been surrounded by the immigration bureau together with the police and the NBI — three agencies. The first wave of fleecing was the NBI and police locking each person in a toilet, because there are no cameras in toilets, and stripping them of everything valuable. The second wave was the immigration bureau negotiating with the company boss for the release of people, with different quotes per person — 1 million, 2 million, 3 million pesos — depending on the mood of the person in charge. That company negotiated at 3 million pesos per person, over 300,000 RMB. The boss ultimately ransomed 30 people, exactly the 30 held on one floor; the rest were promised food deliveries until they got out. This young man ran an operation targeting the Japanese market, scamming middle-aged Japanese women; in his best month he made 2 million RMB, and bought a house and a car in his small hometown county. Later he was kidnapped by a friend, had several hundred thousand transferred away, and was hit with a trumped-up illegal gun-possession charge by a corrupt cop, so he couldn't leave.

points.h: The Philippine lawyer raised his price on the spot when he saw he was Chinese
points.body: In Cebu, through an introduction from a Lithuanian, Feili met a Philippine lawyer who quoted 200,000 pesos, about 20,000-plus RMB, done in four weeks. After Feili got to Manila the lawyer came to visit, saw he was Chinese, and immediately raised the price, saying that was the old price and the new price required another 120,000 pesos, over 10,000 RMB. Feili decided not to use him and wrote off the deposit, turning instead to a Chinese middleman. The Chinese middleman quoted over 30,000 RMB, four to six weeks, no more than six. Feili said the truly reliable Chinese middlemen know this procedure inside out, because everyone locked up in there is Chinese. In the end he was held inside for over thirty days, 41 days total including Cebu. The Lithuanian who'd introduced the Philippine lawyer — when Feili messaged him, he still hadn't gotten out.

quotes.text: Give him 1.5 million pesos now and you can be released immediately, and you'll have no problem at all.
But this isn't about the amount of money. When the phone wasn't in my hands, money was transferred out.

Look at his corrupt bureaucratic system and his ordinary people as separate things. I still believe Filipinos are, by nature, very good people. But the bureaucratic system is truly too corrupt — and it's the kind that drinks blood, human blood.
